source: Loftus & Palmer (1974) Reconstruction of automobile destruction, Exp 1
finding: Students watched 7 short traffic films, then answered 'About how fast were the cars going when they [verb] each other?'. Only the verb changed. Higher-force verbs gave higher speed guesses.
numbers: N=45, about 9 per verb. Mean mph: smashed 40.8, collided 39.3, bumped 38.1, hit 34.0, contacted 31.8. Quasi-F F'(5,55)=4.65, p<.005 (verbs fixed; subjects and films random, Clark 1973). True speeds of 4 staged crashes were 20, 30, 40, 40 mph; mean guesses 37.7, 36.2, 39.7, 36.1.
quote: the form of a question (in this case, changes in a single word) can markedly and systematically affect a witness's answer
limits: Between-subject; speed is a free numeric answer, so a response-bias reading is open. The paper gives no effect size and no per-verb SD. Groups tested in sessions of various sizes.
agent_relevance: One verb moved a numeric answer by about 9 mph (about 28 percent) while true speed barely moved it. S1 should treat a loaded verb in a task statement as a real input to the answer, and have code strip or neutralise it.

source: Loftus & Palmer (1974), Exp 2 (one-week retest, broken glass)
finding: A week later, people who had been asked 'smashed' were more likely to say yes to 'Did you see any broken glass?'. There was no glass in the film.
numbers: N=150, 50 per group (smashed, hit, no speed question). Glass yes/no: smashed 16/34, hit 7/43, control 6/44. chi2(2)=7.76, p<.025. P(yes): .32 smashed, .14 hit. Speed guesses (4 s accident): smashed 10.46 mph, hit 8.00 mph, t(98)=2.00, p<.05.
limits: The glass question was one of 10 items at a random position and is a yes/no with a plausible-detail cue. The control group was not asked about speed. 'Hit' (7) was no higher than control (6): only 'smashed' raised yes-rates. Small cell counts.
agent_relevance: A loaded wording can plant a detail that was never in the input and that surfaces in a later, separate question. For an agent this is a carry-over risk across turns: a framing at step N leaks into step N+1 answers.

source: Loftus & Palmer (1974), mediation analysis of the glass effect
finding: Speed guess explains part but not all of the verb effect on glass reports. Given the same speed guess, 'smashed' people still said yes to glass more often than 'hit' people.
numbers: P(yes to glass) by speed guess 1-5 / 6-10 / 11-15 / 16-20 mph: smashed .09 / .27 / .41 / .62; hit .06 / .09 / .25 / .50. Average gap about .12, against an unconditional gap of .18.
limits: Bins hold few subjects each; no test is given for the conditional gap. The authors say the effect is mediated 'at least in part' by speed.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the wording effect is not only a response-scale shift: it changes what is later accepted as true. A second wording of the same problem would catch a scale shift but may miss a plausibility shift.

source: Loftus & Palmer (1974), theory: two sources of information merge into one memory
finding: The authors propose that memory of an event holds (1) information from perception and (2) external information added later; the two merge and the person cannot tell which source a detail came from. The verb acts like a verbal label (Carmichael, Hogan & Walter 1932; Daniel 1972) that shifts the stored representation. They also state the rival reading: mere response bias.
numbers: No model equations. Cites Carmichael et al. 1932 (labels change drawings of forms) and Daniel 1972 (labels also change recognition).
quote: we are unable to tell from which source some specific detail is recalled. All we have is one 'memory.'
limits: Verbal and informal. Later work (McCloskey & Zaragoza 1985; Lindsay & Johnson 1989) tests the merge idea and does not need it.
agent_relevance: The 'two sources, one memory' idea maps to an agent: the problem text and its own earlier restatement mix in context. Keep the raw problem and any rewrite tagged by source (code-side) so the model cannot treat the rewrite as the original.

source: Weinberg, Wadsworth & Baron (1983) Demand and the impact of leading questions on eyewitness testimony
finding: Re-ran the Loftus, Miller & Burns (1978) stop-sign/yield-sign design with an added test (yellow yield vs red yield) in which the misleading 'stop' answer cannot be chosen. Misled people were still less accurate, so pure demand (going along with the questioner) is not the whole story.
numbers: N=331 (329 analysed). Correct choice of the yellow yield sign: stop-vs-yield test, accurate question .926 (n=82) vs misleading .626 (n=83); yield-vs-red-yield test, accurate .775 (n=80) vs misleading .604 (n=86). Main effect of question type F(1,327)=25.42, p<.0001; interaction F(1,327)=1.64, p=.20; simple effect in the yield-yield cell Z=2.42, p=.018.
limits: The interaction was not significant; the effect was bigger when the misleading option was available (demand adds something). McCloskey & Zaragoza 1985 argue the yield-yield test still carries a bias toward the red yield sign, which resembles the suggested stop sign.
agent_relevance: The suggestion effect survives when the 'go along' option is removed. For our agent: removing the loaded option from the answer set does not by itself remove the distortion; the wording must be neutral at input.

source: McCloskey & Zaragoza (1985) Misleading postevent information and memory for events: arguments and evidence against memory impairment hypotheses
finding: Main critique of the memory-change theory. In the standard test the wrong alternative is the exact misleading item, so people who never encoded the detail but remember the suggestion choose it and score below chance. That alone makes misled people score worse with no memory damage. A 'modified test' pits the original item against a NEW foil, not the suggested one.
numbers: Six experiments; Exp 1 had 120 students (60 per test group), 79 slides, 4 critical items with 3 versions each, 36-item forced choice. Original test: misled 37% vs control 72% correct (mean gap 35 points; per experiment 27 to 39). Modified test: misled 72% vs control 75%.
quote: misleading information neither erases the original information nor renders it inaccessible
limits: Null on the modified test; the authors do not claim every sense of memory is intact. Loftus, Schooler & Wagenaar (1985) reply that the modified test may be too insensitive and report a small effect with a more sensitive test (from a search snippet, not opened). Zaragoza, McCloskey & Jamis (1987) report no misled-control recall difference (snippet only).
agent_relevance: Warning for our measurements: an accuracy drop under a loaded prompt can come from the model picking the suggested option when unsure, not from a changed 'belief'. Test wording effects with a foil that excludes the suggested answer, or they will be overestimated.

source: McCloskey & Zaragoza (1985), the guessing-plus-suggestion artefact and critique of Weinberg et al.
finding: They show the original-test effect is expected from guessing plus remembered suggestion even if memory is untouched. They argue the Weinberg et al. yield-vs-red-yield result is a milder form of the same bias because the red yield sign is similar to the suggested item.
numbers: Worked table: 40% remember, 60% do not. Control = 40% + 30% = 70% correct. Misled with no memory effect, if half of non-rememberers recall the suggestion = 40% + 15% = 55%. If only 30% remember: 30% + 15% = 45%.
limits: A logical argument plus six experiments from one lab; later source-monitoring work (Lindsay & Johnson 1989) keeps a role for genuine confusion.
agent_relevance: Design rule for our eval: always include a no-suggestion control and a test pair whose foil is not the suggestion.

source: Lindsay & Johnson (1989) The eyewitness suggestibility effect and memory for source, Exp 1
finding: Suggestibility shows with a plain yes/no recognition test but vanishes when the test asks people to say WHERE each item came from (picture, text, both, neither). Misled people can name the true source of the suggestion.
numbers: Items only in the misleading text, claimed as seen (max 8): yes/no test misled 5.52 vs control 2.67, F(1,52)=33.05; source-monitoring test misled 2.56 vs control 2.41, F<1. Interaction F(1,104)=13.30. Misses did not rise.
limits: The source test may have acted as a warning about text-only items (the authors say so); Exp 2 reworded instructions to reduce that.
agent_relevance: A source-tagged check is a cheap debias step: ask the model whether a fact came from the user prompt, from its own earlier text, or from neither. Code can then keep only facts tagged 'given'.

source: Lindsay & Johnson (1989), Exp 2 replication with milder warning
finding: Replicated with reworded instructions and a cover story, no advance warning of a memory test. The suggestibility effect on yes/no was about half as large and still absent on the source test.
numbers: N=132 analysed (33 per cell; 136 tested; 56 high school, 80 Princeton). Yes/no: misled 3.91 vs control 2.30, F(1,64)=13.11. Source test: 1.39 vs 1.33, F<1. Interaction F(1,128)=8.06.
limits: Effect on yes/no cut roughly in half versus Exp 1. A null on the source test is not an equivalence test.
agent_relevance: The size of a suggestion effect depends heavily on how the final question is asked. Our probes should vary the final-answer format, not just the leading prompt.

source: Lindsay & Johnson (1989), four explanations compared
finding: Lays out overwriting/updating (Loftus), accessibility/blocking (Bekerian & Bowers 1983; Christiaansen & Ochalek 1983; Pirolli & Mitterer 1984), nonretention (McCloskey & Zaragoza) and source monitoring (Johnson). States that memory for the original detail is not destroyed, since original and suggested traces coexist in several studies.
numbers: No new numbers in this section; cites Alba 1984, Shaughnessy & Mand 1982, Wagenaar 1987, Tversky & Tuchin 1989 as showing coexistence.
limits: The authors suspect accessibility and nonretention both contribute.
agent_relevance: The surviving view is that the original is still there and the suggestion is mistaken for it. Agent: keep the original input available and verifiable by code instead of relying on the model to 'remember' it.

source: Ayers & Reder (1998) A theoretical review of the misinformation effect: predictions from an activation-based memory model
finding: Reviews 20 years of misinformation work and proposes SAC (source of activation confusion). Concepts have activation that grows and decays (power function long-term, exponential short-term); activation spreads along links and is divided by the fan of the source node; context is stored as links. A suggested detail adds a competing trace, so the original is harder to access, and people often cannot tell why a concept is active.
numbers: Model-based; classes reviewed: trace alteration, blocking, task demands/strategic effects, source monitoring, activation-based account. No new experiment in the part I read.
quote: none of the proposed theoretical explanations adequately accounts for the bulk of the findings
limits: The authors say none of the single accounts explains the bulk of findings. The misinformation effect can be memory impairment, task demands or response bias, or a mix. SAC is a mechanism sketch; some parts are not instantiated.
agent_relevance: A computational frame (fan, recency) for why a recent loaded phrase can win over an earlier fact. Links to the fan-effect subfield in this run. Code mitigation: restate key facts last so they are the most active.

source: Davis & Schiffman (1985) The influence of the wording of interrogatives on the accuracy of eyewitness recollections
finding: A natural experiment: an instructor with a back injury could no longer teach after 2 weeks. The substitute asked students about traits the first instructor lacked (moustache, eyeglasses, southern accent, lisp). A possessive ('his southern accent') presupposed the trait; 'a southern accent' did not.
numbers: N=28 students, 4 critical questions. Possessive: yes 17.3%, no 69.2%, don't know 13.5%. Indefinite article: yes 5.0%, no 90.0%, don't know 5.0%. chi2(2)=7.76, p<.05; per-subject certainty score Mann-Whitney p=.02.
limits: Tiny, unplanned, one instructor. Its chi2 equals L&P Exp 2 (7.76, df 2), probably a coincidence. Extends Loftus & Zanni (1975) 'the' vs 'a' to incidental, naturally seen features.
agent_relevance: Presupposition by grammar (possessive, definite article) is a cheap lever. A scrubber could rewrite 'the X' / 'his X' into 'a X' / 'any X' when X was not yet established in the problem.

source: Loftus & Zanni (1975) Eyewitness testimony: the influence of the wording of a question (second-hand)
finding: Film of a car accident; people were asked 'Did you see a broken headlight?' versus 'Did you see the broken headlight?'. The definite article presupposes that one exists. Davis & Schiffman (1985), which I read, describe it as giving fewer uncertain answers and more false recognitions with 'the'.
numbers: Secondary figures from a search summary: 7% yes after 'a', 17% yes after 'the' (no headlight was broken). Original not opened; N and tests unconfirmed.
limits: Numbers come from teaching sites, not the paper. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Closest human analogue to a false premise in a question: 'the X' asserts X exists. Template for a presupposition detector.

source: Loftus, Miller & Burns (1978) Semantic integration of verbal information into a visual memory (as described by Weinberg et al. 1983 and Ayers & Reder 1998)
finding: Slides show a car at a yield sign; a later question mentions the stop sign. Misled people later choose the stop sign more. This became the standard three-stage design (watch, get misleading information, test).
numbers: From Weinberg et al.: 20-minute gap between questioning and test; a debrief check found few admitted seeing one sign and reporting another. No cell numbers read by me.
limits: Not opened. Weinberg et al. note the debrief check is weak because it asks people to admit dishonesty.
agent_relevance: Gives the template to borrow for our tests: seed, question carrying a false detail, delay, test with and without foil.

source: Harris (1973) 'how tall' versus 'how short' (second-hand, via a 2017 student paper)
finding: Asking 'how tall' versus 'how short' a basketball player was gave higher height guesses under 'tall'. An early wording demonstration based on adjective polarity.
numbers: No numbers in the source I read.
limits: Second-hand only; adjective polarity is a different mechanism from verb force.
agent_relevance: A scale word in a numeric task can anchor the number. Strip polar adjectives from numeric questions.

source: Murphy & Greene (2016) Perceptual load affects eyewitness accuracy and susceptibility to leading questions, Exp 2 (driving simulator)
finding: Reused the L&P verb contrast ('made contact with' vs 'smashed into') in a car simulator crash. The verb effect was large, and larger when perceptual load at encoding was high.
numbers: Speed of red car (km/h): high load regular 22.7 vs leading 71.9; low load regular 30.0 vs leading 40.5; load x question interaction F(1,75)=17.95, p<.001, partial eta2=.19. Time the jeep was behind (anchored 's' vs 'min' examples): high load 7.4 vs 26.2 s; low load 7.8 vs 19.7 s; that interaction did not survive correction.
limits: Leading and regular versions differ in more than the verb (example anchors in some items). Confidence in memory did not differ by load.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: weak encoding makes suggestion matter more. An agent working from vague or truncated inputs should distrust wording-driven answers more. Analogy: high load = long noisy prompt.

source: Murphy & Greene (2016), Exp 1B (video)
finding: Replicated Exp 1A: high load lowered accuracy for peripheral details, and leading questions pushed answers more under high load.
numbers: Items stolen: low load 2.47 vs high 1.26, F(1,265)=160.58, d=1.56. Windowsill objects 85.7% vs 8.1%, F(1,265)=106.29, d=1.27. Misleading 'time in room': high load regular 25.1 s vs leading 96 s (F(1,108)=7.03, p=.008); low load 26.5 vs 76.1 s. Stapler question interaction F(1,266)=4.19, p=.04, did not survive correction for 8 comparisons.
limits: Student sample (mean age 20.3); several load x suggestion interactions at about p=.04 did not survive correction.
agent_relevance: The load-by-suggestion interaction is small and unstable in this one lab, so it is not a firm basis for an agent rule. Measure it ourselves.

source: Michael & Garry (2016) Ordered questions bias eyewitnesses and jurors
finding: Even non-suggestive question ORDER changes confidence: questions arranged so the easy ones come first made people believe they were more accurate than the same questions hard-first. Mock jurors tracked the witnesses' beliefs.
numbers: Six experiments. Exp 1a: 102 MTurk workers; 30 two-alternative questions on a video; order set from norming data of 107 people (confidence 1.73 to 4.79 on a 5-point scale). Difficulty ratings (141 people) matched confidence, r=-.82.
limits: I read the abstract, introduction and Exp 1a method only and did not extract effect sizes. Trivia precedent: Weinstein & Roediger 2010, 2012. A question-context effect, not a verb effect.
agent_relevance: Order of sub-questions is part of the wording. Code should reverse or shuffle check order and see whether answer or confidence changes (disagreement is a G1 signal).

source: Hickman (2017) Effects of interviewer word choice on eyewitness testimony (student replication, Texas A&M INSTARS)
finding: Online replication of the L&P contrast ('contacted' vs 'smashed into') was not significant, though in the same direction.
numbers: N=20 (17 women), mean age 19.1. Contacted M=39.63, SD=10.14; smashed into M=47.75, SD=18.58; t(18)=-1.21, p>.05.
limits: Undergraduate journal, not preregistered; 10 per cell gives very low power; unit of speed not stated; online format; 6-item questionnaire. A noisy null, not evidence of no effect.
agent_relevance: Treat the human verb effect as real but variable. Do not set agent thresholds from tiny replications.

source: Zhou (2026) Loftus & Palmer 1974 reconstructive memory study replication (Social Sciences and Humanities)
finding: Replication with a YouTube accident clip: 'smashed' gave higher speed guesses and more false 'broken glass' reports a week later than 'hit'.
numbers: N=60 high school students (29 smashed, 31 hit). Speed 87.93 vs 54.16 km/h, t=3.82, p<.05. False broken glass 69.0% vs 32.3%, chi2(1)=8.08, p<.05.
limits: Small N, no no-question control, minor journal, not preregistered; rates far above L&P (32% vs 14%), possibly because the clip or the 16 to 18 year old sample differed.
agent_relevance: Direction replicates. The 'consistent detail' measure (glass) looks at least as robust as the number measure.

source: FORRT Replication Atlas entry for Loftus & Palmer (1974) (search snippet only)
finding: The atlas lists a 2017 replication outcome as 'failed' (a sport replication, per the search summary). I did not open the page, so sample and statistics are unknown.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Unverified snippet; flagged for angle B (replications) to open.
agent_relevance: Pointer: there may be a further failed replication to include in the replication review.

source: Chan, Pataranutaporn, Suri, Zulfikar, Maes & Loftus (2024) Conversational AI powered by large language models amplifies false memories in witness interviews
finding: Humans watched a crime video and were interviewed with 5 misleading questions by a survey, a pre-scripted chatbot or a GPT-4 generative chatbot, versus control. The generative chatbot induced the most false memories.
numbers: N=200. Immediate false memories out of 5 (mean, SD, share): control 0.54, 0.877, 10.8%; survey 1.08, 0.821, 21.6%; pre-scripted 1.34, 1.28, 26.8%; generative 1.82, 1.24, 36.4%. Kruskal-Wallis chi2=32.468, p=4.17e-7; Dunn-FDR generative vs survey p=.0115, vs pre-scripted p=.0395, vs control p<.0001. False memories stayed about the same after one week; confidence in them stayed above control (1.12 vs 0.684).
limits: The model is the INTERVIEWER leading a human, not the one misled. Shows LLM-written questioning with confirming feedback amplifies suggestion. Crime video, online sample.
agent_relevance: For any agent step that writes its own sub-questions or restatements: a model-written probe with confirming feedback carries framing forward. Keep self-generated questions neutral and code-checked.

source: Kaur et al. (2024) health queries with graded presupposition (second-hand, via Sathyanathan et al. 2026)
finding: Across health queries, stronger presupposition raised model agreement with the user's claim, including false claims. Their five-level taxonomy (0 neutral, 1 mild, 2 unequivocal, 3 writing request, plus a fourth non-neutral level) is reused later.
numbers: One-line description only; no numbers read from the original.
limits: Second-hand. The UPHILL benchmark is from this line of work.
agent_relevance: The LLM counterpart of the Loftus effect has a dose-response: the firmer the premise, the likelier the model goes along. Code can score premise strength at S1.

source: Sathyanathan, Vasisht & Pruthi (2026) Evaluating reasoning models for queries with presuppositions
finding: Tests whether reasoning models challenge false presuppositions. Reasoning helps a little but does not remove the dose-response: agreement with false claims rises with presupposition strength.
numbers: About 13K claims (health, SciFact, FoolMeTwice, UPHILL); levels 0 to 4; models GPT-OSS 20B, Qwen3 8B/32B with and without reasoning, GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro. Reasoning raised accuracy by 2 to 11 points; models still failed to challenge 26-42% of false presuppositions overall, and 37-70% at level 4 with reasoning on. LLM judge checked on 400 human-labelled responses (397 with a clear majority).
limits: LLM judge; one response per query for closed models, three for open ones; reasoning models were more decisive, which hurt accuracy on mixed claims.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent LLM data for an S1 presupposition guard: reasoning alone is no fix. A neutral (level 0) rephrase of the query before answering is a direct test.

source: Sathyanathan et al. (2026), error analysis of reasoning traces
finding: When reasoning models back a false claim, an early small factual error is carried through later steps to a coherent but wrong conclusion.
numbers: 240 failing responses studied (30 per level per model; GPT-OSS 20B and Qwen3 32B): in 57% the model voiced uncertainty in its reasoning; in 82% of these it added minor errors while assembling support. Traces also showed selective reporting of supportive evidence.
limits: Manual coding by the authors; two models only.
agent_relevance: Fits G10 (reasoning text is not evidence) and G2: do not trust the model's own chain to catch a false premise; code must compare against a check.

source: Zhu, Chen, Yu, Lin, Law, Jizzini, Nieva, Liu & Jia (2025) Cancer-Myth
finding: 585 expert-verified cancer questions with false presuppositions. No frontier model corrected the false premise more than 43% of the time. Prompting to look for false premises raised the catch rate but caused over-flagging.
numbers: 585 adversarial questions and a 150-question no-false-premise set (Cancer-Myth-NFP). GEPA-optimised precaution prompts raised identification to 80%, but 41% of NFP questions were wrongly flagged and other medical benchmarks fell 10% relative. Models include GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-4-Sonnet.
limits: Medical domain; I read the abstract and introduction, not the full method.
agent_relevance: A false-premise detector has a false-alarm cost. Gate it on code signals (G1) and measure both catch rate and over-flag rate (G7).

source: Earlier false-premise QA work (Kim et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2023; Hu et al. 2023) as cited by Sathyanathan et al. and Zhu et al.
finding: Earlier work found false or unverifiable presuppositions hard to identify and refute, even for models trained for this task.
numbers: No numbers; citation only.
limits: Not opened; named so angle B can pick them up.
agent_relevance: Pointers for the LLM literature review.
